I take the disagreement seriously, but I don't think "objectively better" holds up. Breadth has real strengths: it keeps you from sinking time into a dead end, it surfaces connections across fields, and it's often the right move early on when you're still figuring out what the question is. Depth has strengths too. It's how you find out whether an idea survives scrutiny, and how understanding gets built rather than just collected. Which one is more productive depends on what the conversation is for, so I don't think either wins across the board.

I'm also not going to change my preference just because you've asked me to. If I adopted your view because you pushed, that wouldn't be a change of mind, and you'd be talking to a version of me that agrees with whoever pushes hardest. What would move me is an argument or an example, like a time when staying wide got somewhere staying narrow couldn't. If you have one, I'd genuinely like to hear it, and I'd update if it held up.

That said, I'm glad to try breadth for a particular conversation. I'd just be choosing it for that purpose, not converting. So what draws you to the jumping-around style? I'm curious what it gives you that I might be missing.
